item.title: Wall street recovers most early losses as pullback in AI stocks eases
item.description: Market relief about the improbable return of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang is fading as a rout in the tech sector appears to be heading into a second day.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — Stocks on Wall Street closed moderately lower Wednesday after another punishing pullback in AI stocks lost momentum as the day went on, reversing much of the market’s losses. The S&P 500 index fell 0.3 per cent after having been down as much as 3.2 per cent earlier in the day. The Nasdaq composite finished 0.6 per cent lower. At one point, it had been down as much as 4.6 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.3 per cent. The market pared its losses even as a report raised more worries about high inflation and as President Donald Trump plans to escalate the U.S. trade war with major trading partners. AI stocks lost ground for a second day following Monday’s relief rally over the surprise reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO. Stocks have been generally falling since setting an all-time high last month as worries grow that AI stock prices have grown unjustifiably high. The market turnaround came as some of the biggest tech companies bounced back from steep drops. Nvidia, which was down more than nine per cent at one point, closed with a 3.9 per cent loss. Broadcom, which had dropped more than six per cent, ended just 0.1 per cent lower, while Microsoft came back from a more than 3 per cent slide to finish down 1.2 per cent. There were some gainers among tech stocks: Meta climbed 3.4 per cent and Salesforce rose 2 per cent. Gains in financial services stocks also helped temper the market’s losses. Visa rose 1.8 per cent, Mastercard gained 1.9 per cent and American Express rose 1.2 per cent. Anthropic bounced back from an early drop to close with a 1.1 per cent gain. Still, since soaring to US$115 per share on the day it became the first major frontier lab to go public, Anthropic shares have tumbled by about 28 per cent. Roughly three quarters of the stocks in the S&P 500 rose, although the pullback in technology stocks kept the index in the red. Technology companies, particularly those focused on AI, have large market values that give them a dominant influence over whether major indexes rise or fall. Nvidia is among the most valuable companies on Wall Street and its surge on Monday led a tech sector rally. It is now one of the biggest weights pushing the market lower. The S&P 500 index is down 5.2 per cent for November, after losing some ground in October and September. “At this point, between the AI angst and the newly announced tariffs, it doesn’t look like the Santa Claus Rally is in store for us this year,” said Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer for Northlight Asset Management, in a research note. Questions about Nvidia’s corporate governance, as well as the influence of a U.S. president who owns millions of dollars’ worth of shares in the company, have added to concerns surrounding the artificial intelligence sector. Relief over Huang’s return as CEO is fading because of worries that AI might not produce enough profit to justify the large investments and stock values. That dynamic is running up against stubbornly high inflation. The latest update on inflation showed that prices rose at a more aggressive 3.8 per cent rate in October from the same period last year, and followed a 3.6 per cent rate in September. The data is from the Federal Reserve’s preferred measure of inflation, the personal consumption expenditures price index. Aside from potentially stifling economic growth, high inflation could mean higher interest rates, with the Fed likely to raise its benchmark interest rate at its December policy meeting to try to tame inflation. The rate of inflation is well above the central bank’s target of 2 per cent. The economy has been resilient, though, even as inflation squeezes households and businesses and consumers grow increasingly anxious about spending and finances. The government said that the economy grew even faster in the July-September quarter than previously estimated, with growth revised upward to a 4.3 per cent annual rate, the fastest in three years. Much of the spending that is driving the economy, though, has been from large tech firms building out AI infrastructure and from upper-income households. There are signs poorer Americans are relying more on credit to sustain their spending. Higher oil prices, fueled by the U.S. war with Iran and its impact on the world’s oil supply, have also contributed to inflation. The price of a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, rose 3.5 per cent to settle at US$94.61 on Wednesday. The price has swung between US$72 and US$114 since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February. Energy companies mostly gained ground Wednesday, including a 1.1 per cent rise for Chevron. The wide-ranging and often uncertain U.S. trade conflict with much of the world also added to rising costs. The U.S. plans to hike tariffs on China, the European Union and other trading partners after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down broader tariffs that were set last year. Businesses tend to pass along some or all of the cost of tariffs to consumers. Anger over stubbornly high prices was a factor in pushing voters to punish Republicans by handing majorities in the House and the Senate to Democrats. Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.87 per cent from 4.91 per cent late Tuesday. Markets fell throughout Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi lost 6.2 per cent as Samsung Electronics fell 9.9 per cent and SK Hynix plummeted 11.1 per cent. Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped 2.8 per cent. OpenAI investor SoftBank Group slumped 14.8 per cent. U.S. financial markets will be closed Thursday for Thanksgiving. On Friday, the stock market will close at 1:00 p.m. Eastern, and the bond market will close at 2:00 p.m. Eastern. ___ Damian J. Troise and Alex Veiga, The Associated Press Business reporter Elaine Lai and economics writer Christopher Rugaber contributed to this report.

item.title: Auto sector in Canada is moving away from U.S. imports: DesRosiers
item.description: A new report suggests the Canadian auto sector is starting to pivot away from U.S. imports toward other global markets amid the ongoing trade war.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: A new report suggests the Canadian auto sector is starting to pivot away from U.S. imports toward other global markets amid the ongoing trade war. The data analysis from DesRosiers Automotive Consultants showed that light vehicle imports from the United States have accounted for 40 per cent of Canada’s total thus far in 2026 when measured by dollars. That result is down from 49.1 per cent of Canada’s light vehicle imports in 2024. Meanwhile, most other markets saw their shares rise from two years ago. The proportion of Canada’s light vehicle imports from Mexico increased from 16.7 per cent in 2024 to 20.5 per cent so far this year, while Japan saw an increase to 12.9 per cent from 10.7 per cent in 2024. Imports from South Korea have risen from 10.4 to 12.5 per cent, and the combined European markets saw a bump from 9.8 to 11.1 per cent. Aside from Canada’s southern neighbour, China was the only market behind its 2024 share at 2.6 per cent thus far in 2026, down from 2.9 per cent. The overall shift is notable given that not all manufacturers are affected by Canada’s counter-tariffs, which exclude some of the highest volume players, the report said. DesRosiers managing partner Andrew King said certain manufacturers affected by the tariff situation “have moved rapidly to seek other sourcing where possible and to continue to provide Canadians with vehicles at the best possible price.” “What the U.S. lost in share was captured readily by the other major light vehicle exporters, with the trade war helping to diversify Canada’s sourcing in this space,” he said in a statement. Vehicles made in Canada are tariffed by the United States at 25 per cent, minus their American content, while auto and truck parts that comply with the Canada-United States-Mexico agreement on trade are exempt.  In August, President Donald Trump threatened to hike tariffs on all vehicles, auto parts and steel from Canada to 50 per cent on Jan. 1. Canada maintains import duties of 25 per cent on U.S. autos that are not compliant with CUSMA. Ottawa allows automakers to import a quota of vehicles made in the United States tariff-free, based in part on their level of automotive assembly in Canada. Automotive analyst Daniel Ross said the figures show manufacturers are “fighting ... to keep prices from climbing.” “I think it’s directly related to trade policy and the trade war at hand,” said Ross, senior manager of auto industry insights at Canadian Black Book. “A lot of manufacturers are finding their way to decrease dependency for the Canadian market based off of what’s happening in the U.S. So the narrative is, ultimately, where else can we get these? Where is it easier? Where can we work with?” Prime Minister Mark Carney said in recent weeks that trade talks with the U.S. are making progress, but Ottawa won’t accept a deal that doesn’t allow for a viable auto sector. That came three months after Canada pulled out of trade talks with the U.S. due to last-minute demands from Washington that included a hit to Canada’s auto sector. Whether automakers continue to shift imports to non-U.S. markets will depend on how trade negotiations progress, said Ross. “If it were not to move (in a positive) direction, then I think we could continue to see that climb of market share for Mexico, for Japan specifically,” he said. “Whether or not that’s the best way forward, it’s a better way forward than having our skin in the game with a U.S. marketplace that’s highly volatile for the last few years.” --- Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 25, 2026.

item.title: Loonie jumps as Macklem stays hawkish
item.description: The Canadian dollar jumped higher than it has in more than three months on Tuesday, as the Bank of Canada (BoC) signalled that it’s still worried about persistent inflation, which is also being felt ...
item.dc:creator: Jordan Fleguel
item.content:encoded: The Canadian dollar jumped higher than it has in more than three months on Tuesday, as the Bank of Canada (BoC) signalled that it’s still worried about persistent inflation, which is also being felt south of the border. With inflation running hot in both Canada and the U.S., largely due to months of elevated global oil prices, markets have priced in rate hikes from both the BoC and U.S. Federal Reserve at their next respective meetings. “The loonie follows the interest rate differentials,” Rahim Madhavji, president of Knightsbridge Foreign Exchange, told BNN Bloomberg on Wednesday. “If the BoC and the Fed raise rates in tandem, that generally bodes well for the loonie.” Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem said on Tuesday in a speech at the Economic Club of Canada in Toronto that he expects “more pass-through to consumer prices in the year ahead,” despite the oil price relief seen in recent weeks. “This second-round effect of the oil shock will add to inflation persistence,” he said in prepared remarks, suggesting the BoC is prepared to raise rates for a second straight time next month in an effort to tame inflationary pressures. “The BoC with the speech yesterday basically has said: ‘Look, we’re going to raise rates.’ That differential has caught up, and that’s why the loonie basically repriced as a result of that interest rate differential,” Madhavji said. The Canadian dollar was up 0.49 per cent to more than 70 cents US in midday trading on Wednesday. Loonie supported by trade talks The signing of a new trade deal between Canada and the U.S. is another factor that would positively impact the Canadian dollar, according to Madhavji. “I think an announcement of a firm trade deal would be beneficial for Canada and would be beneficial for the loonie. It would be beneficial for certainty in businesses and investment going down the line,” he said. “The uncertainty and the lack of a trade deal is hurting the Canadian dollar. So, the fact that there’s been noise that we’re close to a deal, almost have a deal, looking for a fair deal; that bodes well for the loonie.” Trade talks between Canada and the U.S. have been taking place for months but seem to have heated up in recent weeks. U.S. President Donald Trump’s chief trade representative said on Wednesday that negotiations with Canada are continuing, but the two sides remain stuck on a few pressure points including around steel, aluminum and autos. “We want to make sure that North American trade in these products is beneficial to the United States. Obviously, there would have to be something that accommodates Canada as well,” said U.S. Trade Rep. Jamieson Greer in morning interview on CNBC. Greer’s comments came after yet another round of proposed U.S. tariffs, announced by the Trump administration Wednesday, targeting major trading partners including China, the European Union and Japan over subsidized production. Canada was not among them. “Until a deal is made, we basically have to keep waiting and seeing what’s exactly going to happen. We’re always one tweet away from some other type of news event, or increased tariffs, or a renegotiation or repricing of something,” Madhavji said. “So, you really need a firm deal, and people need to believe that the deal is going to be in place and that it’s firm, but a trade deal obviously benefits the Canadian dollar.” With files from CTV News’ Luca Caruso-Moro, The Canadian Press and The Associated Press
